subject: comparing models in INLA, Joint model and simple model with one likelihood.

messages.author: f3efe76710f72d8e
messages.subject: comparing models in INLA, Joint model and simple model with one likelihood.
parts:
Hi
I need your help

I have two kind of model for my data with missing values, one a joint model with two likelihood in inla (Gaussian and Binomial)
and the other one is a model without considering missing data and just one likelihood in inla function.

First question:In joint model output, cpo is a list with 2*n element, i think it's because of two likelihood, with NA values in it for missing values in response y.
How can i compute total CPO for the model for comparing two models?

Second question: Can i ignore NA values in cpo for response which includes missing values in order to compute total CPO?

Do you know if the criterias like DIC,WAIC, marginal likelihood and etc are logical for comparing my two models: joint model with two likelihhood and other one with ignoring missing value?

On Tue, 2018-02-27 at 13:39 -0800, zah.samira wrote:
> Hi
> I need your help
>
> I have two kind of model for my data with missing values, one a joint
> model with two likelihood in inla (Gaussian and Binomial)
> and the other one is a model without considering missing data and
> just one likelihood in inla function.
>
> First question:In joint model output, cpo is a list with 2*n element,
> i think it's because of two likelihood, with NA values in it for
> missing values in response y.
> How can i compute total CPO for the model for comparing two models?

Hi,

yes, its of length 2*n, since this is the length of the linear
predictor.

total cpo. you can add them, this would be the normal approach.
if y[i]=NA, then cpo[i]=NA, so you should ignore them.

>
> Do you know if the criterias like DIC,WAIC, marginal likelihood and
> etc are logical for comparing my two models: joint model with two
> likelihhood and other one with ignoring missing value?

I would not worry about missing values in the response, as DIC and WAIC
are computed for the observed ones only. it should not make a different
either, if you have two different likelihoods.


hope this helps,
H
